title: The shares
hookLine: the inheritance verses set shares for daughters, sons, parents, spouses (4:11–12)

lines: WHO WILL CARE FOR THESE GIRLS?
cards: After Uhud, a widow came to the Prophet ﷺ with her two daughters. Their father, Sa'd ibn al-Rabi', had been killed in the battle, and their uncle had taken everything Sa'd owned.
Commentators describe the old custom: the men who could fight inherited, and women and girls were left out. She asked the Prophet plainly: who will marry these girls with nothing?
The reports say the inheritance verses came down soon after.

teach.h: MIRATH: WHAT IS LEFT TO YOU
teach.b: The word is mirath, inheritance, from a root meaning to inherit, to be left something.
Verses 11 and 12 of an-Nisa set fixed shares, by name. Daughters inherit. Mothers inherit.
Wives and husbands inherit from each other. Parents each receive a sixth when there are children.
A husband receives half of his wife's estate if she has no children, a quarter if she does; a wife receives a quarter, or an eighth.
Sisters and brothers have shares in certain cases. And before anything is divided, the verses repeat, any bequest is honored and debts are paid.

In the story, the Prophet sent for the uncle and told him to give the daughters two-thirds, the mother an eighth, and keep the rest. People often ask about one rule: a son receives twice the share of a daughter.
Classical scholars explain it by duties: in Islamic law, a man must pay the bride's dower and support his wife and family, while a woman's wealth is her own, owed to no one.

Some scholars also point out cases where a woman's share equals or exceeds a man's. Muslims today discuss how these rules apply in modern economies, and families and countries handle them in different ways.

teach.h: UP TO A THIRD BY WILL
teach.b: A hadith in Bukhari adds a limit: a person may leave up to a third by will, and the Prophet said even a third is a lot; better to leave your heirs well off than dependent.

So the shares moved a family's money from whoever was strongest to a list where everyone has a place. This week, from the message outliving the messenger to the shares, has been about what we owe each other.

how: Muslims divide estates according to the shares in 4:11–12 and 4:176, after debts and any bequest of up to a third; the detailed calculation is a field of Islamic law called 'ilm al-fara'id, and many Muslims write an Islamic will.

o: a will that can give away everything
inheritance, the shares left to each heir
the dower a groom pays his bride

p: each parent's share when there are children
the most one may leave by will
his daughters' case came before the verses

s: the inheritance verses leave women out
they name daughters, mothers, wives and sisters, each with a share.
debts are paid before the estate is divided
the verses repeat it: after any bequest or debt.

games.q: you're dividing an estate. there's a large debt. what comes first?
o: give the children their shares first.
pay the debt and honor any bequest, then divide the shares.
split the debt among the heirs.
games.why: debts and bequests first, then the shares, as 4:11–12 repeats.

practice: Think, calmly and as an act of care, about what you'd leave behind if your time came: what you own, what you owe, who depends on you, whether anything is written down. Just notice which answers you don't know yet.

wordCard.voice: Mirath. Inheritance: the shares set out in 4:11 and 12 for daughters, sons, parents and spouses, after debts are paid. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: inheritance, from the root w-r-th, to inherit.

carryVoice: Your line: everyone has a share. Daughters, mothers and wives are named in it. A week, and a new surah well begun.
